A caption is a short piece of text that is attached to something visual — most commonly an image, photo, illustration, chart, or video — to explain, describe, or give context to what you are seeing.

Think of it this way: a visual element (a photo, a picture, a diagram) often cannot speak for itself. It needs words to tell you what it shows, who is in it, when or where it was taken, or why it matters. That explanatory text is the caption.
The Most Common Use: Captions Under Images

This is what most people mean when they say "caption."

When you open a newspaper and see a photograph of a politician shaking hands, there is usually a line of text right below the photo that says something like "Prime Minister Narendra Modi meets with the President of France in New Delhi on Sunday." That line is the caption.

Similarly, in a school textbook, when there is a diagram of the human heart, you will often see text below it saying "Figure 3: The four chambers of the human heart." That too is a caption.

On social media — Instagram, for example — the text a person writes below their posted photo is called the caption. If someone posts a photo of a sunset and writes "Golden hour never disappoints 🌅" — that sentence is the caption.

So in all these cases, the caption is serving the same role: it is brief text that sits close to a visual and helps the viewer understand or appreciate it better.

Key qualities of a caption in this sense:

  • It is short — a sentence or two, rarely more.
  • It is placed near the visual, usually below it, sometimes beside it.
  • It adds information the visual alone cannot give — names, dates, locations, explanations, or even a tone (funny, serious, poetic).
A Second Use: Captions on Screens (Text on Videos)

The word "caption" is also widely used to refer to the text that appears on screen during a video or film to represent spoken words.

When you watch a YouTube video with subtitles turned on, those lines of text appearing at the bottom of the screen as people speak — those are called captions, specifically closed captions. The word "closed" simply means they can be turned on or off by the viewer (as opposed to "open captions," which are always visible and permanently burned into the video).

Captions in this sense serve people who:

  • Are deaf or hard of hearing.
  • Are watching in a noisy environment.
  • Are watching in a language they do not fully understand.
  • Simply prefer reading along as they watch.

So in this context, captions are not about a still image — they are about making a moving video accessible and understandable through text.
A Third (Formal/Legal) Use: The Heading of a Document

In legal and formal writing, the word "caption" has a specific technical meaning: it refers to the heading at the top of an official document, such as a court filing or a legal case.

For example, at the top of a court document, you will often see structured information identifying the case — the names of both parties involved, the name of the court, the case number, and so on. This formal header block is called the caption of the document.

This use is largely limited to legal and official contexts. You are unlikely to encounter it in everyday conversation, but it is worth knowing.

Since learners often confuse related words, here is how "caption" stands apart:

  • Title: A title is the name of something — a book, a film, a section. It identifies the work itself. A caption, on the other hand, describes or explains a specific visual element within the work. The title of a photo album might be "Summer 2024", but the caption under one specific photo might be "Dad and I at the beach in Goa."
  • Label: A label is even shorter and more minimal — it is just a word or brief phrase that names something, like a label on a jar or a label on a map pointing to a city. A caption is more informative and contextual; it says more than just a name.
  • Subtitle: In books and films, a subtitle is a secondary title that supports the main title. In the context of videos, "subtitle" and "caption" are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, but strictly speaking, subtitles translate dialogue from one language to another, while captions transcribe the spoken words for viewers who cannot hear the audio. In practice, many people use both words loosely to mean the same thing.

A caption is text that accompanies a visual — whether that visual is a still image, a diagram, or a video — and its job is to add meaning, context, or clarity that the visual alone cannot provide.

It is always brief. It is always attached to something visual. And it always serves the viewer — helping them understand what they are seeing, who or what is depicted, or what they should take away from it.
